[2025 summer phd math-stat — problem 3]

Part III, Problem 3 (25 pts). Let $\{(X_i, Y_i, R_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ be i.i.d. with covariates $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$, response $Y_i$, and missingness indicator $R_i \in \{0, 1\}$ ($R_i = 1$ if $Y_i$ observed). Assume (a) $Y_i \mid X_i, R_i = 1 \stackrel{d}{=} Y_i \mid X_i, R_i = 0$, and (b) $X_i \mid R_i = 1 \sim P_X$, $X_i \mid R_i = 0 \sim Q_X$ (possibly different). Target: $\beta^* = \arg\min_\beta \mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \mid R_i = 0]$.
(i) Show $\mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \mid R_i = 0] = \mathbb{E}[(Y_i - X_i^\top\beta)^2 \frac{f_{X|R=0}(X_i)}{f_{X|R=1}(X_i)} \mid R_i = 1]$.
(ii) Prove $\frac{f_{X|R=0}(x)}{f_{X|R=1}(x)} = \frac{P(R=0\mid x)}{P(R=1\mid x)}\cdot\frac{P(R=1)}{P(R=0)}$.
(iii) Apply (i) and (ii) to construct an estimator of $\beta^*$.

response.text:
Let

\[
f_r(x):=f_{X\mid R=r}(x),\qquad p_r:=P(R=r),\qquad \pi(x):=P(R=1\mid X=x).
\]

Assume the usual overlap/positivity condition

\[
f_0(x)>0 \implies f_1(x)>0,
\]

so that \(f_0/f_1\) is well-defined on the target support, and assume the relevant second moments exist.

---

## (i) Change-of-measure identity

For fixed \(\beta\), define

\[
m_\beta(x):=\mathbb E\left[(Y-x^\top\beta)^2\mid X=x,R=1\right].
\]

By assumption (a),

\[
Y\mid X=x,R=1 \stackrel d= Y\mid X=x,R=0,
\]

so

\[
m_\beta(x)
=
\mathbb E\left[(Y-x^\top\beta)^2\mid X=x,R=0\right].
\]

Therefore, using iterated expectation,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\mid R=0\right]
&=
\int \mathbb E\left[(Y-x^\top\beta)^2\mid X=x,R=0\right] f_0(x)\,dx \\
&=
\int m_\beta(x) f_0(x)\,dx \\
&=
\int m_\beta(x)\frac{f_0(x)}{f_1(x)} f_1(x)\,dx \\
&=
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\frac{f_0(X)}{f_1(X)}\mid R=1\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2\mid R=0\right]
=
\mathbb E\left[(Y-X^\top\beta)^2
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(X)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(X)}
\mid R=1\right].
}
\]

This is simply a change of measure from the covariate distribution among the missing cases to the covariate distribution among the observed cases.

---

## (ii) Density ratio in terms of missingness probabilities

By Bayes’ rule,

\[
f_{X\mid R=1}(x)
=
\frac{P(R=1\mid X=x)f_X(x)}{P(R=1)}
=
\frac{\pi(x)f_X(x)}{p_1},
\]

and similarly

\[
f_{X\mid R=0}(x)
=
\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)f_X(x)}{P(R=0)}
=
\frac{(1-\pi(x))f_X(x)}{p_0}.
\]

Therefore, for \(x\) such that \(f_X(x)>0\) and \(0<\pi(x)<1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
&=
\frac{\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)f_X(x)}{P(R=0)}}
{\frac{P(R=1\mid X=x)f_X(x)}{P(R=1)}} \\
&=
\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)}{P(R=1\mid X=x)}
\cdot
\frac{P(R=1)}{P(R=0)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{P(R=0\mid X=x)}{P(R=1\mid X=x)}
\cdot
\frac{P(R=1)}{P(R=0)}.
}
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{1-\pi(x)}{\pi(x)}
\cdot
\frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

---

## (iii) Estimator of \(\beta^*\)

From part (i),

\[
\beta^*
=
\arg\min_\beta
\mathbb E\left[
(Y-X^\top\beta)^2 w(X)
\mid R=1
\right],
\]

where

\[
w(x)
:=
\frac{f_{X\mid R=0}(x)}{f_{X\mid R=1}(x)}
=
\frac{1-\pi(x)}{\pi(x)}
\cdot
\frac{p_1}{p_0}.
\]

Thus \(\beta^*\) can be estimated using only the complete cases \(R_i=1\), but with inverse-odds weights correcting the covariate shift between \(R=1\) and \(R=0\).

Let

\[
n_1=\sum_{i=1}^n R_i,\qquad n_0=n-n_1.
\]

Estimate \(\pi(x)=P(R=1\mid X=x)\) using the observed pairs \((X_i,R_i)\), for example by logistic regression or another classifier. Denote the fitted propensity by \(\widehat \pi(x)\). Then define

\[
\widehat w_i
=
\frac{1-\widehat\pi(X_i)}{\widehat\pi(X_i)}
\cdot
\frac{n_1}{n_0}.
\]

The weighted least squares estimator is

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta
=
\arg\min_{\beta}
\sum_{i=1}^n
R_i\widehat w_i
\left(Y_i-X_i^\top\beta\right)^2.
}
\]

Equivalently, when the weighted Gram matrix is invertible,

\[
\boxed{
\widehat\beta
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n R_i\widehat w_i X_iX_i^\top
\right)^{-1}
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^n R_i\widehat w_i X_iY_i
\right).
}
\]

Since \(n_1/n_0\) is constant in \(i\), it does not affect the minimizer; it may be included for estimating the target risk itself, but it can be omitted for estimating \(\beta^*\).

Under standard regularity conditions—positivity, finite second moments, consistency of \(\widehat\pi\), and nonsingularity of the limiting weighted Gram matrix—this weighted complete-case estimator is consistent for \(\beta^*\).
